title: Mineral County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Mineral County well depths run around 80 ft, with most between 50-120 ft. Learn about yields, water levels, drilling costs, and risks before you buy.
h1: Water wells in Mineral County, Colorado
intro_html:
Mineral County is classic high-country hard rock. Most wells are in fractured bedrock, with a few tapping the Unconfined San Luis Vall and alluvial aquifers. Depths and yields are generally favorable, but rock can change quickly from one ridge or valley to the next.

If you’re looking at property outside Creede or closer to the county lines with Hinsdale or Rio Grande County, it helps to understand how deep wells usually go here, how much water they make, what they cost, and what risks to look for before you close on a parcel.

sections.heading: How deep wells go in Mineral County
sections.html:
From the state well records, Mineral County wells are not especially deep for mountain country. The median total depth is 80 feet, and the middle half of wells run from 50 to 120 feet. Only about 6% go between 300 and 600 feet, and around 1% push beyond 600 feet, with the deepest on record at 1,386 feet.

About 59% of wells are under 100 feet, and another 34% land between 100 and 300 feet. That tells you most drill bids will be built around something like a 50–120 foot depth range, but you still plan your budget so you can tolerate hitting one of the less common deeper holes if the fractured rock doesn’t cooperate on your specific lot.

sections.heading: Well yield here: how much water to expect
sections.html:
Yields in Mineral County are generally strong for domestic and small irrigation use. The median reported pump yield is 15 gpm, with the middle half of wells between 10 and 15 gpm. That’s more than enough for a single-family home and normal outdoor use, within the 35 gpm pumping limit for exempt household wells.

Only about 3% of wells fall in the 1–5 gpm range, and none of the reported wells are under 1 gpm. Around 41% are in the 5–15 gpm range, and about 55% are 15 gpm or higher. Still, fractured-bedrock aquifers are uneven, so it’s smart to look closely at nearby well yields on Colorado Well Finder before assuming your new well will match the county median.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they’re doing over time
sections.html:
Static water levels in Mineral County are relatively shallow. The median depth to water is about 35 feet, and the middle half of measurements fall between 10 and 64 feet below ground surface. That usually means modest pumping lifts and lower long-term power and pump wear than you’d see on very deep mountain wells.

Looking at the trend, median static levels were about 27 feet below ground in the 2010s and about 38 feet in the 2020s. That suggests the water table in measured wells has dropped somewhat in recent years. It’s not extreme in the data we have, but it’s a reason to design a system with enough pump setting depth and reserve, and to keep an eye on conditions on your specific property.

sections.heading: Who’s been drilling, and when wells went in
sections.html:
Mineral County has a long history of well construction. State records show 1,519 permits total, with 1,030 wells recorded as constructed and 1,098 reporting a total depth. Drilling picked up in the 1970s and stayed steady for decades.

By decade, there were 10 permits in the 1950s and 7 in the 1960s. Activity jumped to 214 in the 1970s and 184 in the 1980s, then 302 in the 1990s and 303 in the 2000s. The 2010s saw 170 permits, and there are already 131 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2026. The most active drillers in the records are Valley Pump Company (Self, Clinton L.), Irrigation Engineering & Supp. (Burk, Coy), and Larry Burk Drilling (Burk, Larry), so you’ll see those names often in local logs.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Mineral County
sections.html:
Here you’re mostly drilling fractured granite and gneiss, which are slower to drill than soft sediments. Typical drilling rates run around $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 80-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole alone roughly in the $5,200–$8,000 range.

When you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished well at that median depth is usually on the order of $11,200–$20,000. If you’re building a budget, it’s smart to run numbers not just at 80 feet but also out toward 120 or even 240 feet, since the upper tenth of wells extend to around 240 feet and a small share go much deeper.

sections.heading: Risks to watch: low yield, contamination, and siting
sections.html:
The records don’t show many very low-yield wells, but fractured bedrock is unpredictable. Even with a strong county median, one property can still hit tight, low-producing fractures. Plan for the possibility of a lower-yell well and consider storage if you end up closer to the bottom of the 10–15 gpm middle range.

On the environmental side, within about 10 miles there are mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 460 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That doesn’t mean your specific well is unsafe, but it does mean water-quality testing is important. Also keep your well uphill and away from any septic system to protect it, and verify there’s space to meet current setback rules before finalizing a building layout.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Mineral County lot
sections.html:
Most wells in Mineral County are permitted as domestic or household use (about 80%), with some stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells. If you’re buying a home on an existing well, pull the DWR permit and any yield or static level data, and compare it with nearby wells around Creede or closer to Rio Grande and Archuleta County lines.

For vacant land, assume you’ll be drilling into fractured bedrock and budget off the 50–120 foot depth band, with a cushion for going deeper. Ask your driller about the local aquifer they expect to hit, whether that’s unnamed fractured bedrock or the Unconfined San Luis Vall in parts of the county, and get water-quality testing done early in the build so you can design treatment if needed.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Mineral County, Colorado?
faq.a: Based on state records, the median total depth of wells in Mineral County is about 80 feet. The middle half of wells are between 50 and 120 feet deep. About 59% of wells are under 100 feet, and 34% are between 100 and 300 feet. Only a small share run deeper than 300 feet, with the deepest recorded well reaching 1,386 feet.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Mineral County, CO?
faq.a: Reported well yields in Mineral County are generally good. The median pump yield is 15 gpm, and the middle half of wells fall between 10 and 15 gpm. Around 55% of wells report 15 gpm or higher, and about 41% are between 5 and 15 gpm. Only about 3% are in the 1–5 gpm range, and none of the reported wells are under 1 gpm.

faq.q: Are groundwater levels dropping in Mineral County, Colorado?
faq.a: The limited static water level data suggest some decline. Median depth to water across all measurements is about 35 feet, with the middle half between 10 and 64 feet. By decade, the median was about 27 feet below ground in the 2010s and about 38 feet in the 2020s, indicating that water levels in measured wells have tended to be somewhat deeper in recent years.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a water well in Mineral County, CO?
faq.a: In Mineral County’s fractured mountain bedrock, typical drilling rates run about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 80-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone comes out around $5,200–$8,000. A complete system with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical at that depth usually totals roughly $11,200–$20,000, with higher costs if you need to drill significantly deeper than the median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Mineral County, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. Within about 10 miles there are mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 460 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, so water quality can vary. Many homes use well water here, but you should test for basic potability and metals at a minimum, and consider broader testing if you are near historic mining or mapped contamination areas.
